Order 
The present application under Section 582 of BNSS/482 of CrPC has been filed by the applicant seeking quashment of F.I.R. bearing Crime No.352 of 2023 registered at Police Station Morar,
District Gwalior for the offence under Sections 420 and 406 of IPC and subsequent proceedings arising out from the said FIR, if any.

As per prosecution story, the complainant, Mahesh Mittal, son of late Shri Babulal Mittal, aged about 59 years, resident of Garam Sadak, Murar, Gwalior, Madhya Pradesh, who was engaged in the business of scrap trading under the name Mittal Enterprises had alleged that during the course of his business, he came to know through fellow traders that Angel Steel, situated at Amloh Road,
Mandi Gobindgarh, Punjab, Proprietor present applicant/Balwinder Singh through his authorized representative Chetan, son NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:25248 2 MCRC-26624-2023 of Shri Dhoop Singh, resident of Village Julani Khera, Tehsil Kalayat, District Kaithal, Haryana (Pin Code 136117, Mobile No. 9467052170), was offering scrap material for sale.

Upon learning this, the complainant contacted Chetan over the phone to inquire about the material,
its price, and payment terms.
Chetan asked the complainant to come to Panipat, stating that the deal could be finalized after inspection.

Accordingly, the complainant went to Panipat, where Chetan Balwinder Singh vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 8 October, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/190489533/
1 took him to a factory, claiming it belonged to him and the scrap from that factory was for sale.

sentences.text: After negotiations, both parties agreed to a total sale consideration of 1,80,00,000/- (Rupees One Crore Eighty Lakhs) for the entire factory material and machinery.
It was mutually decided that 25,00,000/- would be paid in advance, and the remaining amount would be paid in installments as the complainant lifted equivalent quantities of scrap material.
A written agreement to this effect was executed on 10/10/2022 at Panipat.

Subsequently, the complainant transferred 25,00,000/- on 10/10/2022, 25,00,000/- on 12/10/2022, and 15,00,000/- on 15/10/2022, through RTGS from his Kotak Bank, Murar Branch (A/c No. 0045703126) to the account of Angel Steel, Axis Bank,
Mandi Gobindgarh (A/c No. 921030004100008).
Thus, a total amount of 65,00,000/- was paid by the complainant to Angel Steel.
Against this, he was allowed to lift only three truckloads of scrap material worth 34,66,840/- as per the bills attached.
Thereafter, accused Chetan refused to release further material unless the complainant made full payment of the remaining amount in one lumpsum.
NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:25248 3 MCRC-26624-2023
The complainant protested, stating that payment and lifting were to proceed in proportion as per the agreed terms.
Chetan, however, remained adamant and stopped supplying material.
While the complainant was arranging funds at Gwalior, he was informed that Chetan had already sold the same factory scrap to another party at a higher rate.
When the complainant confronted him over the phone, Chetan admitted this and said that he had received a better offer, therefore, sold it to someone else.
He assured the complainant that he would refund the money within two months.
However, even after more than two months passed, no refund was made.
On demanding repayment, Chetan flatly refused.
On the basis of such allegation, alleged FIR bearing Crime No.0352/2023 was registered against the applicant and other co-accused.

Learned counsel for the applicant has submitted before this Court that the applicant is the sole proprietor of M/s Angel Steel, Amloh Road, Mandi Gobindgarh, Punjab and he is a respectable businessman having deep roots in society and no criminal antecedents.

The present FIR is nothing but a gross abuse of the process of law, as the allegations contained therein arise purely from a commercial transaction and at best, disclose a civil dispute between the parties.

Even if the contents of the FIR are taken at their face value, no cognizable offence is made out and the registration of the FIR is the result of undue influence and pressure exerted by the complainant/respondent No.2.

It is further submitted that the complaint as recorded in the FIR, prima facie and ex facie, manifests only a civil dispute arising out of the contract entered into between the parties and there is no allegation that right from NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:25248 4 MCRC-26624-2023 inception, there existed any intention on the part of the applicant to cheat the complainant.
On the contrary, the complaint itself records that pursuant to the agreement, the complainant lifted three truckloads of scrap material on various dates.
In absence of any allegation of dishonest or fraudulent intent at the time of entering into the agreement, no offence under section 420 of the Indian Penal Code can be said to be made out.
The dispute, if any, relates to performance of contractual obligations and is therefore purely civil in nature.

sentences.text: It is further submitted that the entire transaction between the parties is of a business and commercial character, which has been given a criminal colour for the purpose of exerting pressure and harassment upon the applicant with a view to recover money and such misuse of criminal law for civil recovery has been consistently deprecated by the Apex Court.

In support of his submissions,
reliance was placed on the judgments of the Apex Court in the matters of Vijay Kumar Ghai vs. State of West Bengal, reported in (2022) 7 SCC 124, and Sarabjit Kaur vs. State of Punjab & Others,
Criminal Appeal No. 581 of 2023, decided on 01.03.2023, wherein it was categorically held that a mere breach of contract, in absence of fraudulent intention at inception, does not constitute an offence of cheating or criminal breach of trust.

entities.text: Vijay Kumar Ghai vs. State of West Bengal, reported in (2022) 7 SCC 124
entities.label: PRECEDENT

Sarabjit Kaur vs. State of Punjab & Others,
Criminal Appeal No. 581 of 2023
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Herein case, the transaction in question was one in which time was the essence of the contract and the complainant failed to lift the scrap material and make payment for the same within the stipulated period.

Having failed to perform his part of the contract, the complainant cannot now claim any right to lift the material beyond the contractual period NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:25248 5 MCRC-26624-2023 or to seek refund of the balance amount.
The complaint has been made only as an afterthought when the complainant suffered losses owing to market fluctuations in scrap metal prices.
The FIR has, thus, been lodged maliciously to salvage a failed business deal and to misuse the criminal machinery against the applicant.
Apart from the aforesaid submissions, it is also submitted that all events and transactions mentioned in the FIR took place in Punjab and Haryana.
The agreement was executed, and payments were made, within those jurisdictions.
No part of the alleged cause of action has arisen within Gwalior, Madhya Pradesh.
Therefore, the FIR registered at Police Station Morar, Gwalior, is without territorial jurisdiction and liable to be quashed on this ground alone.

On the basis of the foregoing submissions, it is prayed that the present application be allowed and the FIR in question be quashed along with all consequential proceedings including filing of charge-sheet, as its continuance would amount to abuse of the process of law.

Per contra, learned Panel Lawyer for the State as well as the counsel for the complainant, had opposed the prayer made by the applicant and submitted that the FIR clearly discloses the commission of cognizable offences under Sections 420 and 406 of the Indian Penal Code, as the allegations in the complaint reveal that the applicant and co-accused, acting in concert, induced the complainant to part with a substantial sum of 65 lakhs on the pretext of sale of scrap material, but thereafter failed to deliver the agreed quantity and misappropriated more than 30 lakhs of the NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:25248 6 MCRC-26624-2023 complainant's money and the element of dishonest intention and deception is evident from the conduct of the accused in refusing either to deliver the remaining goods or refund the amount despite repeated demands.

It is further submitted that the plea of the applicant that the dispute is purely civil in nature is misconceived, as the facts demonstrate that the applicant never intended to honour the agreement in its true spirit and had, from the very beginning, planned to cheat the complainant.
The existence of an agreement or part-performance does not wipe out the criminality where dishonest intention can be inferred from subsequent conduct.
The FIR and supporting material thus disclose a clear case of cheating and criminal breach of trust warranting investigation.

sentences.text: It is also contended that questions regarding the intention of the accused and the nature of the transaction are matters of evidence that cannot be adjudicated at the stage of quashing.
The investigation is at a nascent stage, and premature interference would hamper the process of uncovering the truth.
Hence, it was prayed that the application for quashing the FIR deserves to be rejected.
Heard counsel for the parties and perused the record.

In the present case, the dispute between the complainant and the applicant admittedly arises from a commercial transaction relating to sale and purchase of scrap material pursuant to an agreement executed between them.

The record reveals that the complainant had already lifted part of the material and thereafter differences arose concerning payment and delivery, which at best amount to breach of contractual terms and not a criminal NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:25248 7 MCRC-26624-2023 offence.

It is a settled proposition of law that every breach of contract does not constitute the offence of cheating unless fraudulent or dishonest intention is shown to have existed at the inception of the transaction.
Mere failure to keep a promise or to discharge contractual obligations cannot give rise to criminal liability.
Herein case, the FIR itself reflects that the transaction was conducted in the ordinary course of business and payments were made and goods were partially delivered.
There is no material to infer that the applicant had any dishonest intention from the beginning so as to attract the ingredients of Sections 420 or 406 of the Indian Penal Code.

The Apex Court in the matter of Vijay Kumar Ghai and Others v. State of West Bengal and Others,
(supra) has held that criminal proceedings should not be permitted to degenerate into instruments of harassment for recovery of money arising from contractual disputes.

Reference may also be made to the celebrated judgments in the matter of State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal, reported in 1992 Supp (1) SCC 335, wherein the Apex Court has laid down the parameters for exercise of inherent powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C., and in the matter of Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma v. State of Bihar, (2000) 4 SCC 168, the Apex Court was held that the intention to cheat must be present at the time of making the promise and cannot be inferred from subsequent conduct.

has sought to convert a civil dispute into a criminal prosecution.

sentences.text: The present FIR fails to disclose any such intention.

Further, the Apex Court in Delhi Race Club Ltd. v. State of U.P., AIR 2024 SC 4531 has categorically held that offences under Sections 420 and 406 IPC cannot co-exist on the same set of facts, as the essential ingredients of cheating and criminal breach of trust are mutually exclusive.

entities.text: Delhi Race Club Ltd. v. State of U.P., AIR 2024 SC 4531
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: While Section 420 IPC requires proof of dishonest inducement at the inception, Section 406 IPC pertains to misappropriation or breach of trust.
The facts of the present case, even if assumed in the complainant's favour, do not satisfy the ingredients of either offence independently, let alone simultaneously.
Therefore, criminal proceedings cannot be sustained on these allegations.

Accordingly, this Court finds it a fit case to exercise its inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to secure the NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:25248 9 MCRC-26624-2023 ends of justice.

Consequently, the application is allowed, and the FIR bearing Crime No. 352/2023 dated 28.05.2023 registered at Police Station Morar, District Gwalior, for the alleged offences under Sections 420 and 406 of the Indian Penal Code, along with all consequential proceedings arising therefrom, including any charge-sheet or criminal prosecution, is hereby quashed.
